claims.text: Configurational-entropy effects and modified atomic diffusion at nanoscale interfaces jointly govern structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature.
High configurational entropy lowers the thermodynamic driving force for phase segregation.
Nanoscale grain boundaries and interfacial regions act as effective diffusion barriers.
Diffusion barriers at nanoscale interfaces slow atomic migration.
The combination of entropy stabilization and interfacial diffusion barriers maintains a homogeneous, stable microstructure at elevated temperature.
The proposed initial material is a near-equimolar, multiprincipal-element nanocrystalline solid solution with nanoscale grain boundaries and minimal initial segregation.
Heating in the 800–1000°C range can activate atomic rearrangement and reveal chemical or structural instability in HEAs.
Multiscale simulation can provide predictions of atomic diffusion rates for the proposed nanoalloy.
An HEA with engineered interfaces and enhanced configurational entropy will exhibit less grain growth than the baseline during high-temperature exposure.
An HEA with engineered interfaces and enhanced configurational entropy will exhibit less phase separation than the baseline during high-temperature exposure.
An HEA with engineered interfaces and enhanced configurational entropy will retain greater compositional homogeneity than the baseline.
Standard processing that does not target interfacial diffusion barriers produces relatively higher atomic diffusion rates at high temperature.
Standard processing that does not target interfacial diffusion barriers produces relatively greater grain growth at high temperature.
Standard processing that does not target interfacial diffusion barriers produces relatively greater chemical segregation at high temperature.
At substantially lower temperatures than 800°C, diffusion may be too slow for the predicted stabilization contrast to be observed.
At extremely high temperatures, diffusion may overwhelm configurational-entropy stabilization.
Multiscale simulations and preliminary experiments support an interplay between entropy stabilization and interfacial diffusion barriers.
Oxidation and other environmental factors may alter the proposed stability behavior.

Failure of the optimized samples to show significantly reduced grain growth, phase segregation, or loss of chemical uniformity relative to controls would falsify the proposed dominant combined mechanism.
